candidate.answerReason: At most three alterations force either two untouched sums or an equally changed row and column. Four alterations attain six distinct sums, so the minimum is four.

methods.label: Prove a lower bound and attain it
methods.explanation:
Each altered entry affects only its own row sum and column sum. Since all six sums initially equal \(15\), at most one row or column can contain no altered entry. Otherwise two sums would remain \(15\). Thus at least five of the six rows and columns must contain alterations.

Suppose at most three entries are altered. To affect at least five rows and columns, all three rows or all three columns must contain alterations. Interchanging the roles of rows and columns if necessary, suppose all three rows do. There must then be exactly three alterations, one in each row.

At least two columns must also contain alterations. Distributing three altered entries among two or three columns leaves a column with exactly one altered entry. That entry is also its row's only altered entry. If its change is \(d\), both its row sum and its column sum become \(15+d\). They are equal, so three alterations cannot work. At least four are necessary.

Four suffice: change \(4\) to \(5\), \(9\) to \(11\), \(1\) to \(5\), and \(6\) to \(14\), obtaining
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
5&11&2\\
8&5&14\\
3&5&7
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The row sums are \(18,27,15\), and the column sums are \(16,21,23\). All six are different. Therefore the least number of alterations is \(\boxed{4}\), choice \(\mathrm D\).
methods.levelReason: The proof uses elementary counting of affected rows and columns, equal changes in sums, and an explicit construction. No matrix algebra is needed.
